 A federal student loan default can let the government garnish wages, take tax refunds and reduce Social Security, and these 10 points explain the risks and ways out
 1 / 12 List slides Federal student loan default can reach wages, tax refunds and benefits, and 7 more points to know List slides Previous Start over By Colleen Cabili · Updated October 26, 2026 Add QZ to Google Illustration: Quartz
 The federal government can collect on a defaulted student loan in ways most private creditors cannot. When a federal student loan goes into default, the government gains administrative collection tools. It can reach a borrower's paycheck, federal tax refund and Social Security retirement, survivor or disability benefits without first going to court. Those tools are set by federal law, not by a loan contract.
 Default has a specific meaning for federal loans. A federal student loan generally enters default after 270 days of missed payments. Before that point, the loan is delinquent. Once it crosses that line, the government's collection options widen.
 Private student loans work differently. Each private lender sets its own default terms in the loan contract. A private lender cannot use administrative wage garnishment or the Treasury Offset Program. It must sue the borrower and win a judgment before collecting by force. That gap means a student loan default on a federal loan carries different risks than one on a private loan.
 This slideshow walks through 10 points. The first six deal with money the government can take or demand, from wages and tax refunds to the full loan balance and, after a court judgment, bank accounts. Three more describe losses that are not seizures: the borrower options that disappear, the damage to credit and the absence of a deadline for collection. The last slide explains how to leave default through rehabilitation or consolidation. The list is a selection of major consequences, not a complete catalog.
 Collection activity has also shifted in recent years. Involuntary collections on federal student loans were paused during the COVID-19 pandemic. The slides that follow describe what the law allows, not whether a given tool is in use on a given date. The status of any single account depends on its own history. Borrowers unsure whether a loan is in default, or whether collection has begun, can confirm with their loan servicer.
 Wage garnishment of up to 15% of disposable pay 
 Towfiqu barbhuiya / Unsplash
 Once a federal student loan is in default, the Education Department can order a borrower's employer to withhold up to 15% of disposable pay. It does not need a court order to do this. The process is called administrative wage garnishment.
 The garnishment works through the employer, not the borrower. The employer receives a withholding order, deducts the required amount from each paycheck and sends that money toward the debt. The withholding repeats every pay period while the order stays in place.
 Disposable pay is not the same as gross salary. It is the pay left after deductions the law requires, such as income taxes and Social Security and Medicare taxes. The 15% cap applies to that smaller amount.
 A second limit protects lower earners. The borrower must keep weekly disposable pay of at least 30 times the federal minimum wage. If a paycheck is close to that floor, the amount garnished shrinks. At or below the floor, nothing is withheld.
 The order cannot arrive without warning. The borrower must receive written notice before withholding begins, generally 30 days in advance. The notice describes the debt and the borrower's options. Those options include reviewing the loan records, agreeing to a repayment plan or requesting a hearing. At a hearing, the borrower can dispute whether the debt exists or whether the amount is correct. The borrower can also argue that the withholding would cause financial hardship.
 Federal law also limits what an employer can do. An employer cannot fire or discipline a worker because of a garnishment order. An employer that ignores an order can be sued for the amounts it failed to withhold. Borrowers who lost a job involuntarily also get temporary protection. Their wages cannot be garnished until they have worked continuously for 12 months in a new job.
 Private lenders do not have this power. A private lender needs a court judgment before taking any wages.
 Federal tax refunds seized through the Treasury Offset Program 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A defaulted federal student loan can cost a borrower their federal tax refund. Through the Treasury Offset Program, the U.S. Treasury can apply that refund to the unpaid debt before any of the money reaches the taxpayer.
 The program is run by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, which is part of the Treasury Department. Federal agencies that are owed money, including the Education Department, refer delinquent debts to it. When the IRS processes a return that produces a refund, the system checks whether the filer appears on that list of debts. If there is a match, the refund is redirected toward the debt.
 The offset is not limited to a slice of the refund. Garnished pay is subject to a percentage cap. A tax refund offset has no such limit and can take the entire refund if the defaulted balance is large enough. A borrower expecting a refund of several thousand dollars can end up receiving none of it. If the refund is larger than the amount owed, the remainder is paid to the taxpayer.
 Refundable tax credits offer no protection. Refund money that comes from the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit can be included in the offset. The Earned Income Tax Credit is aimed at workers with low and moderate incomes. For a household whose refund consists mostly of these credits, a student loan offset can remove that money entirely.
 Borrowers are supposed to receive a notice before their debt is referred for offset. That notice explains the debt and how to challenge it. Grounds for a challenge include a loan that was already paid or discharged, or one that is not in default. Responding to the notice gives the borrower a chance to dispute the debt before a refund is taken.
 Married couples who file jointly face a specific problem when only one spouse owes the student loan. The spouse who does not owe the debt can file IRS Form 8379, the Injured Spouse Allocation, to claim their share of the joint refund.
 An offset reduces the defaulted balance by the amount taken. It does not, by itself, take the loan out of default. The government's other collection tools remain available.
 Social Security benefits offset for defaulted student loans 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A defaulted federal student loan can reduce Social Security retirement, survivor and disability benefits by up to 15%. The offset cannot push a monthly benefit below $750. Supplemental Security Income is not subject to it.
 This collection tool reaches the monthly income many borrowers depend on later in life. The reduction runs through the Treasury Offset Program. Once a defaulted loan is referred for offset, part of each monthly benefit goes toward the debt before the payment reaches the beneficiary.
 Two limits work together. The first is the 15% cap. The second is the $750 floor. The government can take whichever amount is smaller: 15% of the benefit or the portion of the benefit above $750.
 The difference matters most for people with modest checks. On a $1,000 monthly benefit, 15% equals $150. The amount above the floor is $250, so the offset stops at $150. On an $800 benefit, 15% would be $120, but only $50 sits above the floor. In that case the offset is limited to $50. A benefit of $750 or less cannot be reduced at all.
 The three covered benefit types serve different groups. Retirement benefits go to insured workers who have reached eligibility age. Survivor benefits go to the spouses, children and other dependents of workers who have died. Disability benefits, paid through Social Security Disability Insurance, go to insured workers who cannot work because of a qualifying condition.
 Supplemental Security Income sits outside this offset. SSI is a needs-based program for people with very limited income and resources, including older adults and people with disabilities. The Social Security Administration runs it, but it is a separate program from the retirement, survivor and disability benefits that can be reduced.
 The offset is not limited to people who borrowed for their own schooling. Parents who took out Parent PLUS loans, a federal loan type used to pay for a child's education, carry that debt in their own names. A parent who defaults on those loans faces the same benefit offset rules as any other federal borrower.
 Federal salaries, retirement pay and other federal payments 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A defaulted federal student loan can reach money the government pays out beyond tax refunds. Federal employees can have their salaries offset. Some federal retirement payments and other federal payments can also be reduced and applied to the debt.
 An offset is not the same as a garnishment order sent to a private employer. In an offset, the government is the payer. It reduces a payment it already owes the borrower and puts the withheld amount toward the defaulted loan.
 For federal workers, this means the employer and the creditor are both arms of the same government. A federal employee with a defaulted student loan can have part of each paycheck redirected to the balance through a process called salary offset. No outside company has to be ordered to cooperate.
 Salary offset comes with procedural protections set out in federal law. Before deductions begin, the employee is entitled to written notice of the nature and amount of the debt and of the agency's intent to collect through pay deductions. The employee can also inspect and copy records related to the debt, propose a voluntary repayment agreement and request a hearing to contest it.
 The Treasury Offset Program handles many of the other payments. The program is run by the Bureau of the Fiscal Service, part of the Treasury Department. Federal agencies refer delinquent debts to it. The program then checks those debts against federal payments due to go out. When a scheduled payment matches a person with a referred debt, the program can reduce that payment.
 Some federal retirement payments can be reached as well. That matters for borrowers who left government work with a loan still in default. Social Security benefits fall under separate offset rules of their own.
 Not every federal payment is treated the same way. Whether a given payment can be offset, and how much of it, depends on the type of payment. A borrower who sees a federal payment reduced can ask the loan holder which debt the offset was applied to.
 These offsets stay possible for as long as the loan remains in default.
 Full loan balance due at once plus collection costs 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Once a federal student loan goes into default, the government can demand the entire unpaid balance immediately instead of in monthly installments. This step is called acceleration. Collection costs can also be added on top of what the borrower already owes.
 Before default, the borrower owes a scheduled monthly amount under a repayment plan. Acceleration ends that arrangement. The debt is no longer treated as a series of payments stretched over years. It is treated as one sum that is due now.
 That shift changes what it takes to fix the problem. A delinquent borrower can usually return to good standing by paying the missed amounts. Once the balance is accelerated, catching up on past-due payments is no longer enough on its own.
 The accelerated amount covers more than the money originally borrowed. It includes the outstanding principal along with interest that has built up on the loan. Interest does not stop when a loan defaults. It keeps accruing on the unpaid principal. As a result, the balance can grow even while the borrower makes no payments at all.
 Collection costs are a separate charge. The promissory note a borrower signs for a federal student loan allows the costs of collecting the debt to be charged if the loan goes into default. Those charges are added to the balance the borrower must repay.
 For a borrower trying to settle the debt, the figure needed to clear it is the principal plus accrued interest plus any collection charges. A borrower can request that payoff figure from the loan holder.
 Acceleration also shapes how the government's other collection tools work. With the full balance due, collection is not limited to a missed monthly amount. Garnished wages, offset tax refunds and reduced federal benefits can all be applied toward the whole accelerated debt.
 The balance does not have to stay accelerated permanently. Loan rehabilitation and consolidation both return a borrower to a regular repayment arrangement. Collection costs can still affect the final amount owed under either route.
 Bank accounts and property after a court judgment 
 Illustration: Quartz
 The federal government can sue a borrower over a defaulted student loan. A court judgment can then lead to the seizure of money in bank accounts or a lien on property. The Education Department cannot empty a bank account on its own authority without first winning a judgment.
 That requirement separates litigation from the administrative tools used against defaulted federal loans. Wage garnishment, tax refund offsets and Social Security offsets run through agency and Treasury processes. A bank account seizure or a property lien runs through a court.
 A federal lawsuit begins when the government files a complaint and serves it on the borrower. The borrower then has a set period to respond. A borrower who ignores the papers risks a default judgment, meaning a ruling entered without the borrower's side being heard. Responding keeps open the chance to dispute the amount owed, raise defenses or negotiate.
 The U.S. Department of Justice represents the federal government in court. Federal collection lawsuits are generally filed in federal district court.
 A judgment gives the government more ways to collect than it had before. The exact remedies depend on federal law, state law where it applies, and the procedures the court follows. Under those rules, a creditor holding a judgment may be able to garnish funds held in a bank account. It may also record a lien against real estate, such as a house.
 A lien does not necessarily force an immediate sale. It attaches the debt to the property. That can complicate selling or refinancing until the debt is paid or the lien is released.
 Some money and property can be shielded from collection under exemption rules. Which assets qualify varies by law and by the type of creditor. The protections available depend on the rules that apply to the specific case.
 A judgment does not make the debt go away. The balance remains owed, and interest can continue to build after the court rules.
 This court route is also the main path open to private student loan lenders. Without the government's administrative tools, a private lender reaches bank accounts only through a lawsuit and a judgment.
 Losing deferment, forbearance and new federal student aid 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A defaulted federal student loan cuts off the relief tools borrowers normally rely on. In default, a borrower can no longer use deferment or forbearance to pause payments. The borrower also loses eligibility for new federal student aid until the default is resolved.
 Deferment and forbearance are the standard ways to put federal loan payments on hold. Deferment is tied to specific circumstances, such as enrolling in school at least half-time, unemployment or economic hardship. Forbearance is a temporary pause or reduction that a servicer can grant when a borrower faces financial difficulty.
 The two options treat interest differently. During deferment, the government generally pays the interest on subsidized loans. During forbearance, interest keeps building on every loan type.
 Before default, these options can keep a struggling borrower in good standing. A job loss or a large medical bill does not have to turn into missed payments if a pause is approved in time. After default, that route closes. A borrower whose income drops cannot use deferment or forbearance to halt payments on the defaulted debt. The loan stays in default status.
 The loss of new federal student aid affects anyone planning to return to school. Federal aid includes Pell Grants, federal Direct Loans and Federal Work-Study. A defaulted federal loan blocks eligibility for all of them. The restriction applies whether the goal is a degree, a certificate program or graduate study. A borrower hoping to finish an interrupted degree may have to cover tuition from other sources or delay enrolling.
 These restrictions last until the borrower addresses the default. Paying the loan in full ends it. Loan rehabilitation and consolidation are the two main programs that bring a defaulted loan back into good standing. Each has its own requirements. Once a loan is no longer in default, the borrower can again request deferment or forbearance. The borrower can also apply for federal aid again by filing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as the FAFSA.
 Private student loans follow different rules. Any payment pause on a private loan depends on the lender's own contract terms rather than federal programs.
 Credit report damage from a student loan default 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A federal student loan default is reported to the credit bureaus, and the record can stay on a borrower's credit report for years. That entry can make borrowing, renting and opening new accounts harder and more expensive.
 Credit reports in the U.S. come mainly from three national bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Lenders and other businesses pull these reports to see how a person has handled past debts. Common credit scores, including FICO and VantageScore, are calculated from the data in those reports. Payment history is a central input to both.
 A default can follow a borrower into any application that involves a credit check. Mortgage lenders, auto lenders and credit card issuers use credit reports to decide whether to approve an application. They also use them to set the interest rate. A borrower with a default on file may be turned down or offered a higher rate. Over the life of a mortgage or car loan, a higher rate means more money paid in interest.
 Landlords often review credit reports when screening rental applicants. A default can lead a landlord to reject an application or ask for a larger security deposit or a co-signer. Utility and phone companies may also check credit before opening service and can require a deposit up front.
 A private lender can report missed payments to the credit bureaus too. A borrower with both federal and private loans can end up with negative entries from more than one creditor.
 Borrowers can see what has been reported by requesting free copies of their reports from each of the three bureaus through AnnualCreditReport.com, the site authorized under federal law. A lender may not report to every bureau, so the three reports can differ. Errors can be disputed with the bureau that lists them.
 The default label is not always permanent. Leaving default through loan rehabilitation removes the default status from the loan. A borrower weighing that route can ask the loan servicer how the account will appear on credit reports afterward.
 No statute of limitations on federal student loan collection 
 Illustration: Quartz
 Federal student loans have no expiration date for collection. Congress removed the time limits on collecting these debts in 1991. The rule applies across federal loan programs, including Direct Loans, older Federal Family Education Loan Program loans and Perkins Loans. The government can keep pursuing a defaulted federal loan for as long as it remains unpaid.
 Most consumer debts work differently. A credit card balance or an unpaid medical bill can become too old to sue over once a state's statute of limitations runs out. A defaulted federal student loan never reaches that point. A balance that went into default decades ago carries the same legal weight today as one that defaulted last year.
 In practice, waiting does not make the debt go away. Once a loan is in default, the passage of time does not weaken the government's right to collect. A borrower who stopped paying in their 20s can still face collection in their 50s or 60s.
 The lack of a deadline also covers the government's collection tools. Administrative wage garnishment remains available against a debt that defaulted long ago. The Treasury Offset Program, which can intercept federal tax refunds, has no cutoff for older loans either. Social Security benefits can also be offset. A loan taken out in early adulthood can resurface decades later, when a borrower starts collecting retirement benefits.
 Private student loans fall under a different framework. They follow each lender's contract terms. Private loans are generally subject to state statutes of limitations on debt collection. Those time limits vary from state to state. The federal government faces no such limit.
 For a borrower with an old federal loan, age offers no protection. Ignoring a defaulted federal loan does not run out the clock. The routes that end involuntary collections are resolving the default through loan rehabilitation or consolidation, or paying off the balance. Without one of those steps, the default stays in place and collection can continue.
 Getting out of default through rehabilitation or consolidation 
 Illustration: Quartz
 A defaulted federal student loan can return to good standing through loan rehabilitation or loan consolidation. Rehabilitation takes nine on-time payments within 10 months and removes the default status. Either route can stop involuntary collections such as wage garnishment and Treasury offset.
 Rehabilitation is a repayment agreement the borrower has to keep. Each of the nine payments must arrive on time, and all of them must fall inside a 10-month window. That leaves room for one month without a qualifying payment. A second missed month within the window makes the target impossible to reach.
 The rehabilitation payment is calculated from the borrower's income rather than from the full balance. The aim is a monthly amount the borrower can afford. A borrower with very low income can end up with a small payment.
 Completing rehabilitation ends the default itself, not just the collection activity. The record of the default is also removed from the borrower's credit history. Late payments reported before the loan defaulted stay on the report.
 Rehabilitation is generally available only once per loan. A borrower who rehabilitates a loan and later defaults on it again cannot use the same route a second time.
 Consolidation works differently. A new Direct Consolidation Loan pays off the defaulted loan, and the borrower owes the new loan instead. The defaulted debt is replaced rather than repaired through a run of payments.
 Consolidating a defaulted loan comes with conditions. One option is to agree to repay the new loan under an income-driven repayment plan. The other is to make three consecutive, voluntary, on-time, full monthly payments on the defaulted loan before consolidating.
 Consolidation can be the faster exit. It does not erase the default from the credit report, though. The old loan is reported as paid off through the consolidation, but the record of the default remains.
 The two routes trade time against credit history. Consolidation can end garnishment and offsets sooner for a borrower who needs relief quickly. Rehabilitation takes most of a year but leaves a cleaner credit record behind.
 The loan holder can confirm which route applies to a specific loan and what each one requires.
